question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ to the canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}.$
current_example.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=4, \quad$ $\lambda_2=2, \quad$ and $\quad\lambda_3=1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For $\lambda_1=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/ee346f5c2588e633e695b54ec24b2adb6deb0078456fe1fd9ee55e9e2a1ab5f3.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/7d55147b165a6505c450cdfec39afae95890629bd07c7ef4db24a491f335160d.svg)

- For $\lambda_2=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/f9af033fb62376e1590308f35380c2b35e4693d075fa84ef79b3f424afcf0e45.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/6afb7dc4faecb26e1d54dc823b152f31b1d581857fdcf047b1c915b7e8e0a7c4.svg)

- For $\lambda_3=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/318e27c04a6e4d943f5dec0c933ff072c89fad1ad7cddc6b18f87a140b3f2299.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_3$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_3  \| = 1,$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/14c6a31a905412a6bb56b2ec3f0608856fa8b9a4495302d8d18b8dfc71da7a25.svg)

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:
